analyses.title: Revisiting Joint Modeling of Cross-document Entity and Event Coreference Resolution
analyses.research_question: Can cross-document entity and event coreference be improved by jointly and iteratively modeling the dependencies between event mentions and their entity arguments rather than resolving the two tasks independently?
analyses.methodology: The authors build an iterative neural coreference architecture that alternates between entity and event clustering, updating each mention representation using the current clusters of semantically related mentions of the other type. Mention representations combine lexical span features, ELMo context, and predicate-argument information, and separate neural pairwise scorers drive agglomerative clustering. The system is trained and evaluated on ECB+, using gold mentions, document topic clustering, and standard MUC, B3, CEAF-e, and CoNLL F1 metrics. Joint and disjoint variants, prior systems, deterministic baselines, ablations, and manual error analysis are compared.

key_findings.finding: The joint model achieved 79.5 CoNLL F1 for event coreference, 10.5 points above the previously published KCP result and 1.0 point above the authors' disjoint model.
For entity coreference, the joint system obtained 71.2 CoNLL F1, compared with 70.0 for the disjoint variant and 67.4 for the Cluster+Lemma baseline.
Joint modeling improved both entity and event coreference over the disjoint architecture, with the reported differences significant under bootstrap and permutation testing at p<0.001.
Document topic pre-clustering was itself highly consequential: adding the authors' clustering stage to KCP improved its event-coreference CoNLL F1 by 4.6 points.

Ablation experiments showed that representations of semantically dependent mentions contributed more than the simple pairwise binary joint features, while removing both joint components reduced event CoNLL F1 from 79.5 to 78.5.

Error analysis showed that the same cross-type dependencies that improve performance can propagate mistakes, including errors originating from predicate-argument extraction or incorrect entity/event clusters.

limitations: Evaluation is restricted to ECB+, a relatively small news-domain corpus whose annotations cover only selected salient mentions.
The experimental setup uses gold entity and event mentions rather than performing end-to-end mention detection.
Training uses gold topic clusters and gold within-document entity clusters, whereas inference relies on predicted document clusters and an external within-document entity-coreference system.
Predicate-argument information depends on semantic-role labeling and heuristics, and extraction errors can propagate through the joint iterative clustering process.
There were no previously published ECB+ entity-coreference results under the same setup, limiting direct comparison for the entity task.
Strong performance partly depends on unusually effective topic clustering on the ECB+ test set, so gains may not transfer unchanged to less clearly separated document collections.
raw_claims: The model alternates between entity and event clustering instead of resolving them independently.
Event representations can use information from current entity clusters, and entity representations can analogously use event clusters.
Mention representations combine lexical span, contextual, and semantic-dependency information.
The disjoint architecture already substantially improves over the previously published ECB+ event-coreference result.
The joint architecture adds a smaller but statistically significant improvement over the disjoint architecture.
Topic clustering makes a strong contribution to event-coreference performance on ECB+.
Continuous representations of semantically related mentions contribute more than the binary joint features alone.
Incorrect cross-type clustering decisions can propagate between entity and event resolution.
Predicate-argument extraction errors are one source of downstream clustering errors.
The implementation was released publicly by the authors.

analyses.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
analyses.research_question: How can a pre-trained deep neural classifier be augmented with a rejection mechanism that guarantees, with high probability, a user-specified selective risk while retaining as much prediction coverage as possible?
analyses.methodology: The paper formulates selective classification in terms of risk and coverage and introduces the Selective Guaranteed Risk algorithm, which selects a confidence threshold using finite-sample probabilistic risk bounds. Two confidence-ranking mechanisms are evaluated: maximum softmax response and Monte Carlo dropout. Experiments use VGG models on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and VGG-16 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet, with held-out samples used to select thresholds and independently assess achieved risk and coverage.

key_findings.finding: The proposed procedure provides a high-probability selective-risk guarantee for a fixed classifier and confidence-ranking function, targeting Pr(R>r*) below the specified confidence parameter delta.
Softmax response and Monte Carlo dropout produced similar risk-coverage profiles on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, while softmax response was substantially better on ImageNet.
On CIFAR-10, a target risk of 1% produced test risk 0.92% with test coverage 78.56% at delta=0.001.
For ImageNet top-5 classification with ResNet-50, a target risk of 2% produced test risk 1.89% while retaining 59.35% coverage.
Across the reported risk-control experiments, the observed test risks remained below the corresponding computed bounds.

The experiments demonstrate the central selective-classification trade-off: large reductions in classification error can be obtained by abstaining on lower-confidence examples, at the cost of reduced coverage.

limitations: The method starts from a separately trained, fixed classifier rather than jointly optimizing the predictor and rejection function.
The theoretical guarantee assumes the calibration examples are sampled i.i.d. from the same underlying distribution relevant to deployment.
Achievable coverage depends on how well the selected confidence score ranks correct versus incorrect predictions.
Only standard 0/1 classification loss is studied.
The empirical study is limited to image classification on CIFAR and ImageNet and does not test distribution shift or non-image domains.
The paper identifies joint training of the classifier and selection mechanism as an important unresolved problem.
raw_claims: Selective classification allows a model to abstain rather than predict every example.
The paper represents selective performance through the relationship between risk and coverage.
The proposed algorithm chooses a confidence threshold intended to satisfy a requested risk bound with high probability.
Maximum softmax response serves as a simple confidence-ranking function.
Monte Carlo dropout is evaluated as an alternative uncertainty-based ranking mechanism.
Softmax response and Monte Carlo dropout behave similarly on the two CIFAR datasets.
Softmax response is clearly stronger than Monte Carlo dropout on the reported ImageNet experiments.
On CIFAR-10, very low selective error is attainable while retaining a substantial fraction of examples.
ImageNet experiments show that the same approach works with both VGG-16 and ResNet-50.
The paper leaves simultaneous optimization of prediction accuracy and selective coverage for future work.

analyses.title: Case notion discovery and recommendation: automated event log building on databases
analyses.research_question: Can candidate case notions for process mining be automatically discovered from complex databases and ranked by predicted event-log interestingness before the expensive event logs themselves are constructed?
analyses.methodology: The authors formalize database-oriented case notions using the OpenSLEX meta-model and define procedures for deriving case identifiers and event logs from connected database structures. They define structural event-log quality or interestingness measures and inexpensive predictors based on case-notion and dataset characteristics, implementing the workflow in the open-source eddytools package. Evaluation uses an SAP sample dataset containing 87 tables and generates 10,622 candidate case notions; actual generated logs provide ground-truth metric values. Prediction accuracy and recommendation quality are compared with regression and learning-to-rank methods, including fivefold cross-validation and NDCG@10.

key_findings.finding: The framework can systematically generate alternative database case notions and construct corresponding event logs, allowing multiple process perspectives to be explored from the same underlying data.
The authors' unsupervised predictors were substantially less accurate for individual log-property values than stronger supervised regressors such as quantile regression and neural-network regression.

Despite weak absolute prediction accuracy, the custom unsupervised predictor preserved relative interestingness well enough to provide useful rankings and outperformed the evaluated regressors on average for ranking quality.
Among the compared supervised ranking approaches, MART and Random Forest were the only algorithms whose median NDCG@10 exceeded the custom predictor's median in the reported comparison.

When labeled training data are available, supervised regressors are preferable for accurate property prediction and learning-to-rank methods such as Random Forest and MART provide stronger rankings; the proposed predictor is intended for settings without such training data.

The SAP evaluation generated 10,622 case-notion candidates from 87 tables, illustrating the combinatorial search problem that motivates predicting promising views before materializing every event log.

limitations: The proposed definition of log interestingness uses only structural properties such as support, level of detail, and average events per trace.
The interestingness metric ignores business semantics, activity meaningfulness, and behavioral homogeneity.
The relationship between the objective interestingness score and subjective judgments from business analysts or domain experts was not evaluated.
Individual predictions of event-log properties lack accuracy even when the resulting relative ranking is useful.
The approach assumes that the database schema and the locations or representation of events are already known, so event-data discovery itself still requires domain knowledge.
The main quantitative evaluation uses a single SAP sample dataset, limiting evidence for generalization across substantially different database environments.
raw_claims: Different ways of correlating database objects and events produce different process-mining case notions.
The framework represents these correlations formally so candidate event logs can be generated automatically.
The authors evaluate candidate logs using structural characteristics intended to represent interestingness.
Predicted interestingness can be calculated without first building every candidate event log.
The evaluation produces 10,622 candidate case notions from an SAP dataset containing 87 tables.
The custom unsupervised predictors are weak at estimating exact event-log property values.
Relative ranking quality is considerably better than the absolute prediction accuracy would suggest.
MART and Random Forest provide stronger rankings when suitable training data are available.
The unsupervised custom predictor remains useful because it requires no labeled training set.
The eddytools package implements the data preparation, case-notion discovery, and event-log building workflow.
The paper explicitly treats its structural definition of interestingness as incomplete and in need of user-centered validation.

analyses.title: Cross-document Event Coreference Search: Task, Dataset and Modeling
analyses.research_question: Can cross-document event coreference be reformulated as large-scale semantic search from a single query event mention, and can retrieval-plus-reading models effectively find and extract its coreferring mentions across a large document collection?
analyses.methodology: The authors define Cross-document Event Coreference Search and construct CoreSearch from manually validated WEC-Eng clusters augmented with roughly one million Wikipedia-based distractor passages per split. They adapt the Dense Passage Retriever architecture using SpanBERT encoders, explicit event-mention boundary markers, hard BM25 negatives, and a retriever-reader pipeline. A DPR-style reader is compared with an integrated reader whose passage score explicitly models pairwise event coreference. Retriever and end-to-end performance are evaluated using MRR, mean average precision, recall, exact match, and F1, followed by ablations and qualitative error analysis.

key_findings.finding: CoreSearch establishes a query-oriented alternative to exhaustive cross-document event clustering, in which a marked event mention is used to retrieve and extract all coreferring mentions from a large passage collection.
The dense SpanBERT-based retriever outperformed the BM25 baseline across the reported retrieval metrics.
On the test set, the integrated end-to-end model achieved MRR@10 of 90.06, mAP@10 of 63.26, mAP@50 of 72.91, exact match of 71.44, and span F1 of 84.16.
Explicit mention-boundary markers provide a strong signal, improving retriever performance and particularly helping mention-span detection in the reader.
Replacing the generic DPR passage-selection score with an explicit coreference-scoring component improved both passage reranking and mention detection.
key_findings.section: 5.4 Ablation Study - Modeling Coreference with QA

key_findings.finding: Manual analysis of 18 genuinely erroneous top-ranked results found 10 argument-inconsistency errors and 8 cases where the local query and candidate contexts were insufficient to decide coreference.
The authors publicly released both the CoreSearch dataset and their implementation.

limitations: CoreSearch inherits annotation noise from WEC-Eng, especially because the original WEC-Eng training portion was automatically annotated.
The Wikipedia-derived corpus may contain duplicated or otherwise imperfect documents that were not comprehensively audited.
Negative passages can occasionally contain unannotated true coreferences, producing false negatives.
The benchmark is biased toward events sufficiently notable to have Wikipedia coverage and therefore excludes many anecdotal or routine real-world events.
The benchmark is English and Wikipedia-centric, so robustness in workplace communication, news streams, private records, or other domains remains untested.
Error analysis indicates that local passages may be insufficient when event identity depends on global cluster information or external knowledge.
raw_claims: The paper recasts cross-document event coreference from exhaustive clustering into query-based retrieval.
A query consists of an event mention marked inside its surrounding passage.
Positive results are passages containing mentions of the same underlying event.
CoreSearch is derived from manually validated WEC-Eng clusters and large collections of distractor passages.
Each CoreSearch split contains roughly one million candidate passages.
The retriever uses a DPR-style dual-encoder architecture with SpanBERT representations.
Explicit tokens around the target event mention help the model focus on the queried event.
Training includes hard negatives retrieved by BM25 as well as in-batch negatives.
The reader both reranks retrieved passages and extracts the candidate coreferential mention span.
An explicit coreference score improves the DPR-style reader.
Argument mismatches are a prominent source of false coreference decisions.
Some event-identity decisions require evidence outside the local pair of passages.
The authors released CoreSearch and the associated code.
